task_brief: This is day 5 of "Patterns, Sequences, and Introductory Algorithms". That is unit 4 in grade 3. Today is a mastery demonstration about finding and fixing a mistake in steps. It takes about 40–60 minutes. It is one day's work, not the whole unit project. Your unit is working toward this: Write and test a step-by-step set of directions for a partner or character to follow. Today helps by working on finding and fixing a mistake in steps. Your unit also covers what is an algorithm, everyday sequences, giving step-by-step directions, and following a partner's directions. Today counts for a grade. Do it on your own.
primary_task: Show that you can do this on your own: finding and fixing a mistake in steps. Put away the help sheet and the examples. Solve a new problem all the way. First write what answer you expect. Then test it two ways. Include one tricky case. Show what you expected and what you got. Then explain your thinking. Write it so someone new to finding and fixing a mistake in steps could follow it. Everything you need is printed in activity_setup. It has the exact case, what should happen, how to try it, checks, and a paper choice worth the same score. Do not wait for another handout or app. Keep today's work tied to your unit. Today is about finding and fixing a mistake in steps. It is part of "Patterns, Sequences, and Introductory Algorithms". Later days in this unit cover other things, like what is an algorithm. Before you stop, do this check: Rate confidence in finding and fixing a mistake in steps, cite one piece of evidence from today, and choose: ready to extend, ready to review later, or need a different explanation. In grade 3 you need one clear try with a grown-up nearby. Say or write your reason in a sentence or two. Drawings, objects, or spoken answers are all fine.

concept_teaching.title: Evidence before edits: finding and fixing a mistake in steps
concept_teaching.entry_check: Before reading, write one prediction about finding and fixing a mistake in steps and one observation that could show the prediction is wrong. This readiness record is no-penalty evidence.
explanation: finding and fixing a mistake in steps is about making a clear choice and showing why it works. First name what the result should do. Then point to the step, label, or fact that supports your choice.
A check is different from a guess. Write what you expect before you try it. Compare what happened with what you expected. If they differ, circle the first place they stop matching.
A fix needs a reason. Change one thing that your evidence supports, try the same checks again, and keep the old and new work. That record shows your thinking even when the first try was wrong.

Use a state table before touching the artifact: expected state, actual state, first divergence, cause hypothesis, one controlled revision, and a complete rerun. You may use paper, objects, labelled drawings, or precise steps when a computer is not the best tool.

debugging_reasoning.title: Use the six-move evidence cycle
required_moves: Symptom: record expected versus actual without explaining it away.
Hypothesis: state one falsifiable cause about the claim or design state before revising.
Inspection: identify the first trace row or printed detail that bears on the hypothesis.
Predicted effect: state what one controlled change should alter and what it should leave unchanged.
Test and interpretation: compare actual with the prediction and mark the hypothesis supported, rejected, or not fully tested.
Verification: rerun all relevant checks and record any new limitation or next hypothesis.
debugging_reasoning.anti_guessing_rule: A working final artifact without a pre-change hypothesis and inspectable evidence is incomplete debugging/revision evidence.

remediation: Reteaching for finding and fixing a mistake in steps follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for finding and fixing a mistake in steps, model it with a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the process for finding and fixing a mistake in steps works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of finding and fixing a mistake in steps, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking finding and fixing a mistake in steps mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply finding and fixing a mistake in steps under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or teach the idea with an original example without completing another learner’s graded work. Treat this as optional depth on finding and fixing a mistake in steps rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays inside the same sandbox rules — no real credentials and no live external systems. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
